title: EU watchdog probes Commission’s AI pick over conflict of interest concerns
content:
The EU’s watchdog is investigating whether the European Commission managed to “identify, assess and address” actual or potential conflicts of interest when it appointed the chairman of Siemens as Ursula von der Leyen’s AI envoy.

A group of NGOs complained in June to the European Ombudsman about the choice of Jim Hagemann Snabe. Among his responsibilities in the role is to produce a report on issues including AI infrastructure, frontier AI technologies and industrial AI adoption. 

The NGOs, which include Transparency International and Corporate Europe Observatory, warned that Snabe’s ongoing role at Siemens “may compromise the envoy’s independence and impartiality.”

The European Ombudsman in September launched a probe into the Commission over its failure to respond to the NGO concerns.

Now, it has gone one step further.

“You argue that the Commission did not properly identify, assess, and address actual or potential conflicts of interest,” Ombudsman Teresa Anjinho wrote in a letter to Corporate Europe Observatory. “Therefore you would like the Commission to revoke the appointment.”

creator: Mari Eccles

title: EU needs only ‘very trusted partners’ on AI chips, tech chief says amid Nvidia crisis
content:
LISBON — The European Union should work “only with very trusted partners” on artificial intelligence microchips, its tech chief said Tuesday, just days after revelations of a spy scandal rocked industry leader Nvidia.

“When we speak about very critical technologies, like AI semiconductors and quantum technologies, cybersecurity, satellites … it’s very important that we are working very closely only with very trusted partners,” said Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission’s executive vice president for tech sovereignty. She made the comments in an interview with POLITICO at the Web Summit tech fair in Lisbon, when asked about Europe’s reliance on Nvidia.

It is Virkkunen’s first public comment since Nvidia opened an internal investigation into whether its CEO was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation. Top executive Jensen Huang admitted to an affair following a reported relationship with an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed whom the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

creator: Pieter Haeck, Laura Greenhalgh

title: Prince Harry slams ‘lawless’ social media’s impact on children
content:
BRUSSELS — Royalty descended on the European Parliament on Tuesday as Prince Harry slammed Big Tech for creating a world of “chaos.”

“A handful of very powerful people … would like to see the world as a social media world: lawless, no consequence, complete chaos, division,” the Duke of Sussex said at an event on online safety for children.

Speaking in a room packed to the brim with journalists and photographers, Harry called for stricter rules on social media platforms to protect kids from content that could lead to suicide or self-harm.

He expressed reservations about the privacy policies of social media platforms, which he said bar parents from knowing how their children died. “That cannot be right,” a visibly upset Harry said.

His wife, Meghan Markle, was present but withdrew from an address on Tuesday’s panel.

The European Commission regulates online platforms through its Digital Services Act and is planning a special regime for minors under the Kids Act.

The burden of proof that platforms are safe should be on the companies rather than on parents, and “the EU Kids Act is exactly that,” said the prince, praising an EU proposal that would bar access to social media for under-13s.
snippet: BRUSSELS — Royalty descended on the European Parliament on Tuesday as Prince Harry slammed Big Tech for creating a world of “chaos.”
creator: Eliza Gkritsi

title: Europe needs Nvidia. It’ll take more than a spy scandal to change that.
content:
BRUSSELS — Last month, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang got Europe’s full red-carpet treatment from the likes of King Charles, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Now it’s crickets.

As an alleged Chinese spy scandal engulfs the man running the world’s dominant AI microchips producer, potentially awkward questions loom for European leaders in both the public and private sectors who rubbed shoulders and inked deals with Huang. But the silence also reflects the cold economic and strategic reality that Europe has no homegrown alternative to Nvidia.

A German government spokesperson said Monday in response to a barrage of questions on the upheaval at Nvidia that it “does not comment on the media reports,” and that “we always adhere to the highest standards, including when agreements are being reached.” A European Commission spokesperson also had no comment on the matter.
snippet: BRUSSELS — Last month, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang got Europe’s full red-carpet treatment from the likes of King Charles, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
creator: Pieter Haeck

title: Spain’s conservatives promise to relax climate rules if they win election
content:
MADRID — Spain’s center-right People’s Party has pledged to “put a stop to the imposition of unrealistic timelines” for climate goals if it wins the national elections on Nov. 29, a significant pivot from the Sánchez government’s pro-green policies.

The PP, the favorite to win the vote, said decarbonization is an “essential goal for Europe,” but promised to push for an “orderly, realistic, and fair transition,” according to the energy chapter of the party’s manifesto obtained by POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook.

The manifesto said it’s time “to reassess the pace of progress” in the clean energy transition “without dogmatism,” while conceding there are “environmental, geostrategic and economic reasons” behind the decarbonization strategy.

Spain under Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has been one of the bloc’s most influential cheerleaders for ambitious climate goals, advocating to protect key EU policies like the Emissions Trading System, pollution reduction targets and the phase-out of gasoline cars.

But the PP’s manifesto shows that would change if the EU’s fourth-largest economy votes for a conservative government led by PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo.
snippet: MADRID — Spain’s center-right People’s Party has pledged to “put a stop to the imposition of unrealistic timelines” for climate goals if it wins the national elections on Nov. 29, a significant pivot
creator: Nacho Alarcón, Diego Rodríguez Veiga

title: EU countries still can’t get it together on AI
content:
BRUSSELS — As European leaders prepare to project urgency at their first joint meeting on artificial intelligence, their governments are missing important AI safety and infrastructure targets.

The bloc’s 27 leaders are meeting Friday in Dublin to discuss how to accelerate efforts to stay safe and be more competitive on artificial intelligence.

Yet 16 capitals have missed a deadline to appoint a national authority to enforce the bloc’s AI safety law, and Brussels has also pushed back an effort to support the buildout of data centers because of national administrative delays.

European Parliament lawmaker Sergey Lagodinsky, a German member of the Greens, said the delays are undermining capitals’ credibility when speaking about Europe’s AI ambitions.

“Stop blaming the EU for missing the race if you miss your own deadlines,” he said. “Europe’s AI ambitions cannot be delivered if national capitals cannot get their act together.”

In a letter seen by POLITICO, Lagodinsky asked the European Commission to start a formal procedure against capitals for failing to meet their legal requirements under the AI law.
snippet: BRUSSELS — As European leaders prepare to project urgency at their first joint meeting on artificial intelligence, their governments are missing important AI safety and infrastructure targets.
creator: Pieter Haeck

title: Mélenchon squares up to Brussels in election manifesto
content:
PARIS — French leftist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon wants a radical overhaul of EU rules that would set him on a collision course with Brussels.

The far-left leader, who has enjoyed a recent surge in the polls ahead of the 2027 election, pitched a series of measures to fundamentally rethink the EU’s agenda in his presidential platform unveiled Friday. Mélenchon also said he would disobey current EU rules that would prevent him from implementing his platform if elected.

Proposing a “new deal” for Europe, Mélenchon wants to redraft the treaties, ditch core parts of the EU’s rulebook — including debt and deficit limits — suspend competition rules for public services such as energy, transport and telecoms, and loosen state aid laws.

“We will immediately implement our program at the national level. This will therefore require a confrontation with European institutions,” according to the manifesto from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed. “This also means disobeying rules blocking [us] whenever necessary.”
snippet: PARIS — French leftist presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon wants a radical overhaul of EU rules that would set him on a collision course with Brussels.
creator: Marion Solletty

title: EU accuses TikTok of designing algorithm that creates ‘rabbit holes’
content:
The European Commission has accused TikTok of violating its online platforms rules for having designed algorithms that lead users down so-called rabbit holes.

The preliminary findings announced Friday mark the first time the Commission has focused on a social media platform’s recommender systems as a breach of its powerful Digital Services Act, under which it can issue fines up to 6% of a company’s annual global revenue.

“This is the first time that we are really tackling head-on the engagement-based recommender system model,” said one Commission official, who was granted speaking anonymity to speak freely.

This is the fifth case of the EU executive accusing TikTok of breaching EU rules, even though it has issued no fines against the Chinese-owned platform.

In Friday’s announcement, the Commission says the company didn’t adequately consider the risk of sending users down “rabbit holes” through a “continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image.”

The investigation focused on mental health impacts because “the evidence was strongest,” when asked about how these rabbit holes contribute to radicalization, said another official.
snippet: The European Commission has accused TikTok of violating its online platforms rules for having designed algorithms that lead users down so-called rabbit holes.
creator: Eliza Gkritsi

title: France, US clash over G7 effort on AI safety
content:
The U.S. government has scuttled a French push for the G7 to coordinate on advanced AI safety, with a White House official calling it “unnecessary bureaucracy.”

France’s digital minister Anne Le Hénanff told a French Senate hearing on Wednesday that she held two ministerial meetings in September and October to secure G7 commitments to a high-level working group to test frontier AI — the most advanced models — and share information about risks and incidents.

That effort “did not reach a successful conclusion” because the U.S. wanted to pursue its own approach, the French minister said.

“They are not prepared, at this stage, to issue a joint statement with the other six G7 nations, and have asked us to wait for the findings of their own assessment,” said Le Hénanff. “Naturally, we regret this, but we are continuing to move forward as Europeans on this issue.”

A White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that the French government proposed a “poorly defined body” to cooperate on AI that the administration feared would “create unnecessary bureaucracy.”
snippet: The U.S. government has scuttled a French push for the G7 to coordinate on advanced AI safety, with a White House official calling it “unnecessary bureaucracy.”
creator: Milena Wälde, Brendan Bordelon, Émile Marzolf

title: Mélenchon’s mission for his young fans: Debate boomers on Facebook
content:
PARIS — Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s campaign has a plan for winning over older French voters: get his young supporters to sign up for Facebook to talk to their parents.

Mélenchon, 75, may be the oldest candidate in next spring’s race to replace Emmanuel Macron. But his progressive platform and call for a civic revolution have made him a hit with younger voters, who are more likely to scroll through TikTok and Snapchat than through the old-school social network.

“We’re strong [on every other social media platform],” said Antoine Léaument, who handles the Mélenchon campaign’s communication operations. “Facebook is one of the places where the digital battle could be decisive.”

More than 40% of voters younger than 35 plan to vote for Mélenchon, according to a recent Cluster17 poll commissioned by POLITICO. That figure drops to 14% or less across the age brackets over 50 — groups that, if they use social media at all, tend to favor Facebook over its newer rivals.

According to Médiamétrie, France’s leading audience measurement company, platforms like Instagram and Snapchat have 35% more daily users than Facebook among 15-to-24-year-olds.
snippet: PARIS — Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s campaign has a plan for winning over older French voters: get his young supporters to sign up for Facebook to talk to their parents.
creator: Victor Goury-Laffont

title: EU budget battle paralyzes Brussels on AI chips, the Arctic and agriculture
content:
BRUSSELS — Europe’s push to accelerate AI chip production and plan to strengthen its Arctic presence are among the key EU policy files caught in the logjam of Brussels’ seven-year budget standoff.

European policymakers say they can’t move forward on their files without sufficient visibility on proposals linked to EU funding, as the negotiating impasse over the size of the EU’s 2028-2034 budget means financial allocations after next year are unknown.

“There’s an increase in sectoral legislation with objectives that require multiannual budgetary commitments,” said a person involved in talks on the EU budget, who was granted anonymity to discuss closed-door negotiations. “But the budget talks are disconnected from the policy discussions.”

EU governments are racing to find a deal among themselves over the total size of the money pot by the end of the year. The so-called frugal countries pushing for major budget cuts — Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Denmark and Finland — have publicly said that a proposal by the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU envisioning €159 billion cuts doesn’t go far enough.
snippet: BRUSSELS — Europe’s push to accelerate AI chip production and plan to strengthen its Arctic presence are among the key EU policy files caught in the logjam of Brussels’ seven-year budget standoff.
creator: Pieter Haeck, Marianne Gros, Gregorio Sorgi

title: Russia denies involvement in fridge hacks across Europe
content:
A spokesperson for the Kremlin denied on Thursday that Russia had any involvement in the cyberattacks affecting supermarket refrigerators, calling the allegations “absurd.”

Dmitry Peskov said accusations of Russian involvement in the attacks are “unfounded,” according to reports in Russian media. These allegations are “becoming a persistent trend in European countries,” he added.

Supermarket refrigerators have been hacked in multiple European countries over the past few weeks, forcing retailers to throw away thawing fresh and frozen food. The attacks also hit French blood banks, though the country’s blood collection service said its supplies were not affected.

While pro-Russian hacker groups claimed the attacks on Wednesday, it is notoriously difficult to attribute a cyberattack to a specific actor definitively, and those groups quickly deleted the claims, according to the BBC.
snippet: A spokesperson for the Kremlin denied on Thursday that Russia had any involvement in the cyberattacks affecting supermarket refrigerators, calling the allegations “absurd.”
creator: Sam Clark

title: ‘Stop using US tech’: EU lawmaker says Starlink service cutoff led to deaths
content:
“Stop using U.S. tech. That’s my message,” Finnish EPP lawmaker Aura Salla declared Thursday at the European Pulse Seminar.

In an interview with POLITICO, Salla argued that last month’s speed cap on the SpaceX military Starshield service in Ukraine was “yet another example of a kill switch,” which in this case led directly to battlefield deaths.

“We are losing lives in Ukraine. It’s about our defense, because defense is technology.”

Salla issued her stark warning as a pushback against Brussels’ growing focus on AI adoption over building frontier models in Europe. In her Sept. 16 State of the Union address, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: “We do not need to be the ones who develop the frontier technology to be the ones who draw the greatest value from it.”

Salla argued that Europe needs frontier models to have “any room in these negotiations,” over the direct of artificial development and safety. Leading French frontier lab Mistral has likewise warned that Europe will be shut out from shaping AI without a player leading development of the most advance models.
snippet: “Stop using U.S. tech. That’s my message,” Finnish EPP lawmaker Aura Salla declared Thursday at the European Pulse Seminar.
creator: Milena Wälde, Pieter Haeck

title: Metsola tells MEPs not to rely on AI when drafting laws
content:
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola warned MEPs Wednesday not to be overreliant on AI in decision-making, as the Parliament prepares new guidelines for lawmakers on how to use it.

“Drafting an amendment with the help of AI cannot replace fundamentally the constructive debate with a colleague,” she said at an event on AI use in the Parliament. “Doing legal research with the help of AI cannot ultimately replace the judgment and the critical thinking needed to make a tough decision.”

Metsola said there must be “democratic accountability” in lawmaking and argued that “where AI is used, people should know.”

“No matter how AI may be used in a parliament, the responsibility is still [with] those who are elected,” she said.

Secretary-General Alessandro Chiocchetti said at the same event that Parliament is building its own AI tool for sensitive work, hosted on its internal infrastructure.

As POLITICO reported in July, commercial AI models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Meta’s Llama, can still be used for less sensitive tasks.
snippet: European Parliament President Roberta Metsola warned MEPs Wednesday not to be overreliant on AI in decision-making, as the Parliament prepares new guidelines for lawmakers on how to use it.
creator: Max Griera

title: Commission turns to artificial intelligence to write better laws
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission is now using artificial intelligence to draft new laws and simplify existing ones, it said in an annual review of progress on its ongoing simplification drive.

As part of a major plan to cut red tape and administrative costs for businesses, the EU is making deep reforms to how it creates and enforces rules on everything from tech, agriculture and migration to environmental protection and taxation.

To do that, the Commission is deploying new digital tools internally to “modernise” lawmaking. The tools aim to help its staff “identify similarities across legal acts, pointing at potential overlaps, inconsistencies or duplicates, as well as opportunities for simplification,” it said in an annual simplification report presented on Wednesday.

According to the document, the Commission is also beefing up legal training and staff to make sure new rules are not overly complex.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The European Commission is now using artificial intelligence to draft new laws and simplify existing ones, it said in an annual review of progress on its ongoing simplification drive.
creator: Marianne Gros

title: Nvidia hires Wachtell Lipton for Jensen Huang investigation
content:
Nvidia hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead an investigation into reports that CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation.

Law firm partner Joon H. Kim will lead the probe. Kim, a former acting attorney of the Southern District of New York, was appointed in 2021 as an independent investigator by New York Attorney General Letitia James to probe allegations of sexual harassment by former Gov. Andrew Cuomo.

The company’s board of directors on Sunday launched an independent investigation into Jensen Huang following reports of his romantic relationship with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy. The board said that Jensen Huang supports the review.

Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang was first brought to light in an October New York Times report, which alleged the businesswoman had ties to Chinese intelligence. Officials suspected Alice Huang helped funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China, according to the report.

Jensen Huang in a message to the company Sunday admitted to an affair and pledged to cooperate with the investigation. He did not mention Alice Huang by name.
snippet: Nvidia hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead an investigation into reports that CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation.
creator: Katherine Long

title: Brussels takes on the evils of online commerce
content:
BRUSSELS — You know that customer-service bot that won’t let you cancel your subscription? The EU wants to kill it.  

With a new law presented Wednesday, the European Commission will take aim at the endless array of practices websites have used over the past 20 years to make more money from consumers.  

The Digital Fairness Act is the European response to a wider regulatory trend that has seen consumer authorities curb irksome and exploitative practices. These include dynamic pricing that changes ticket prices based on demand, cumbersome processes for canceling subscriptions and the near-complete surrender of customer service to automated systems.  

According to a draft of the DFA obtained by POLITICO, the Commission will address several aspects of the design, service and terms under which businesses interact with consumers online. 

“Europe should not accept a digital economy where profits depend on exploiting people’s vulnerabilities,” Spanish socialist lawmaker Laura Ballarín Cereza, a key European lawmaker on tech legislation, said in a statement.
snippet: BRUSSELS — You know that customer-service bot that won’t let you cancel your subscription? The EU wants to kill it.
creator: Eliza Gkritsi

title: UN experts warn of Big Tech influence over Ireland’s digital oversight
content:
United Nations-appointed human rights experts have contacted the Irish government to raise concerns about the independence of the country’s privacy regulator and the financial barriers to class actions, citing the risks of “undue influence” from Big Tech firms.

The experts said on Wednesday that the independence of data protection authorities and effective access to courts are “essential to safeguarding the right to privacy, particularly where powerful technology companies are involved.”

Many tech giants including Apple, Google, Meta and Microsoft have their European headquarters in Ireland, making the country’s privacy regulator, the Irish Data Protection Commission (DPC), the lead European enforcer for EU privacy law.

Irish government authorities have long faced criticism for being too lax on tech giants, whose presence is critical to the country’s economy. Last year, the appointment of Niamh Sweeney, a former lobbyist for Meta, as Ireland’s data protection commissioner reignited criticism from civil society over “the perception and reality of the DPC’s independence.”

The privacy regulator and the government have consistently denied any claims of undue influence.
snippet: United Nations-appointed human rights experts have contacted the Irish government to raise concerns about the independence of the country’s privacy regulator and the financial barriers to class
creator: Ellen O'Regan

title: Brussels sets slimline legislative agenda for 2027
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission is scaling back its legislative ambitions for 2027, prioritizing competitiveness, deregulation and economic security as the clock starts to run down on Ursula von der Leyen’s second term. 

According to its annual Work Programme and related annexes obtained by POLITICO, the EU wants to strengthen the single market, cut red tape, modernize industry and bolster its defense capabilities at a time of mounting geopolitical risks and economic uncertainty. 

The Commission released the final version of the program and annexes on Wednesday.

“The EU must retain the ability to forge its own path,” the Commission says, adding that “independence is our priority for Europe’s economy.” 

But with existing initiatives — such as the Industrial Accelerator Act — facing delays, Brussels is focusing on getting legislation that is already in preparation across the finish line. 

It’s also killing off proposals that have no chance of passing, along with a crop of outdated regulations — including one on sales of butter stocks to the long-defunct Soviet Union.  

Here are the key initiatives from the Work Programme, due to be announced Wednesday:

title: EU Commission to probe supermarket cyberattacks
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission will assess how well supermarkets are prepared to handle cyberattacks after refrigerators in dozens of stores across at least six EU countries were taken offline.

EU Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen told POLITICO that the attacks would be discussed at the next meeting of its Security College to assess retailers’ contingency plans and their ability to respond to incidents.

“Europe’s food supply chain must be prepared for new and evolving threats,” Hansen said. “The repeated cyberattacks on supermarkets are deeply concerning, causing economic losses for retailers and empty shelves for consumers.”

The announcement follows dozens of supermarkets across Europe reporting disruptions to their refrigeration and freezing systems on Monday.

Incidents were reported in at least six EU countries — Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia — with some retailers reporting that refrigerator temperatures had suddenly surged to as high as 50 degrees Celsius.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The European Commission will assess how well supermarkets are prepared to handle cyberattacks after refrigerators in dozens of stores across at least six EU countries were taken offline.
creator: Gerardo Fortuna

title: Mistral CEO: Europe faces ‘complete trap’ without frontier AI
content:
BERLIN — Europe risks falling into a “complete trap” if it focuses on industrial AI while leaving frontier models to the U.S. and China, Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch said in an interview Monday.

On the sidelines of the Digital Summit in Berlin, Mensch said Europe needs to build its own computing capacity and advanced AI models to ensure security. He added that Europe cannot assume it will always have access to the most powerful foreign models, pointing to the risk that the U.S. and China could deploy export controls on AI.

“The idea that we can build anything meaningful without owning the foundation of it, which are the reasoning models, the brains that can operate the factories, that can help design better systems … is, I think, a complete trap,” he said. “And we’re lucky that people realize this now, that this is not a viable way.”

In recent weeks, Mensch has emerged as a leading voice against European leaders’ shift away from building frontier AI models. In September, top EU leaders advocated building applications on foreign models to reap the benefits, instead of chasing frontier models.
snippet: BERLIN — Europe risks falling into a “complete trap” if it focuses on industrial AI while leaving frontier models to the U.S. and China, Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch said in an interview Monday.
creator: Larissa Kögl

title: Berlin unveils blueprint to catch up on AI
content:
BERLIN — Germany is unveiling its plan to catch up in the global AI race, but key details remain unclear.

Germany should become a “sovereign AI nation” by 2030 and narrow the gap with leading AI hubs in the U.S. and China, according to a report drafted by the government’s AI task force and obtained by POLITICO set to be released Monday.

“The next 12 to 18 months will therefore be decisive in setting the course,” read the report, which was due to be presented to the National Security Council and also at a summit on AI in Berlin.

Germany wants to secure access to the world’s leading models while strengthening European alternatives, particularly through expanded cooperation with France and Canada, according to the report. 

“We are leveraging collaborations with like-minded partners in the EU and worldwide (especially France and Canada) to benefit the German AI ecosystem and ensure sovereign access,” the report noted. “We will also use intra-European collaborations,” such as with French AI company Mistral, “to achieve this leverage,” its authors added.

At the same time, “AI made in Germany” should stand out through its focus on industrial AI with “highly specialized models,” the report read.
snippet: BERLIN — Germany is unveiling its plan to catch up in the global AI race, but key details remain unclear.
creator: Larissa Kögl

title: Modern warfare spurs demand for new medical techniques
content:
Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s health system and the changing nature of warfare have prompted innovative ways to protect wounded soldiers on the battlefield. 

From drone injuries and evacuations to fears of chemical, biological, nuclear or radiation attacks, there’s a major need for new technology and techniques to better support fighters — and citizens — caught in modern war zones.

Although banned under international law, attacks on health care facilities have become commonplace. The Kremlin has attacked health care facilities more than 3,000 times since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to World Health Organization data — and it continues to destroy critical health supplies.

In addition, double tap strikes — when a second attack is launched against people going to help those injured in the first — have also increased the risks health care personnel face on the battlefield. 

These new warfare tactics serve to psychologically break those fighting to protect Ukraine, former U.S. Navy SEAL Marcus Luttrell said. “To completely break down the society, you get rid of the energy and then the health care,” said Luttrell, a former Navy medic.
snippet: Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s health system and the changing nature of warfare have prompted innovative ways to protect wounded soldiers on the battlefield.
creator: Dominic Giannini, Claudia Chiappa

title: EU and Canada’s 6-month test of commitment
content:
MONTREAL, Canada — The European Union and Canada have agreed to build the closest possible relationship. Over the next six months, they will have to define what that means — and whether Canada can become the EU’s first, and perhaps only, associate member.

A summit in Montreal last week highlighted the urgency behind the budding relationship. Both sides say their partnership is positive and not directed against any country. But it is also driven by mutual need: to shore up supply chains, pool expertise and reduce reliance on the United States and China.

Mark Carney told POLITICO in an interview straight after the summit that the two sides should not be tailoring their partnership to cope with the potential reactions of other powers. “We’re not adjusting [based on] what the U.S. might think, what China might think, what … Russia might think,” he said. The goal, the Canadian prime minister explained, is to help both sides “withstand shocks” and prevent rivals from exploiting critical dependencies.

title: Forget AI, Europe has a plan to win the next tech revolution
content:
Draft strategy on quantum computing obtained by POLITICO shows Europe won’t repeat its AI regulatory playbook.

By PIETER HAECK
in Brussels

Illustration by Nicolás Ortega for POLITICO

A perennial also-ran in the global AI race, Europe now sees an opportunity to win what promises to be another technological revolution by learning from its mistakes.

Brussels is set to unveil the Quantum Act, a major piece of tech-sector legislation aimed at pushing EU countries to band together to attempt to stay ahead of the United States and China in quantum computing.

A draft of the November proposal obtained by POLITICO seeks to overcome factors that have constrained Europe’s ambitions in artificial intelligence, including a lack of funding to turn research into commercially viable and competitive products — and to scale globally.

Crucially, it also shifts focus away from regulating the technology to driving competitiveness — an acknowledgement of concerns that Europe overregulated AI and shouldn’t do the same in a field in which it is at the scientific forefront.
snippet:
Draft strategy on quantum computing obtained by POLITICO shows Europe won’t repeat its AI regulatory playbook.

By PIETER HAECKin Brussels

title: 8 things we learned at the EU-Canada summit
content:
MONTREAL — Prime Minister Mark Carney wanted the landmark EU-Canada summit to be about much more than “nomenclature.” He got what he craved. 

Over a whirlwind 48 hours in Montreal, top officials from Brussels and Ottawa huddled to pursue agreements on critical minerals, super computers and defense cooperation.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Carney gathered as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to upend the global order and Chinese dominance of critical markets squeezes middle powers. 

Those challenges have pushed the EU and Canada into a rapidly developing partnership that eclipses anything attempted by Brussels with a non-member country since the bloc was formed. 

Here are all the key things POLITICO learned during the EU-Canada meetings. 

Initially reluctant, the Canadian prime minister came around by the end of the summit to endorse von der Leyen’s controversial label for the global alliance the EU and Canada are building. 

Carney set a six-month deadline to firm up the ground rules of what “associate membership” is, trialing an induction process that could be a model for other non-European countries.
snippet: MONTREAL — Prime Minister Mark Carney wanted the landmark EU-Canada summit to be about much more than “nomenclature.” He got what he craved.
creator: Ben Makuch, Zi-Ann Lum, Mike Blanchfield, Nick Taylor-Vaisey, Jacob Parry, Zoya Sheftalovich

title: Mark Carney puts deadline on EU ‘associate membership’ push
content:
MONTREAL — Canada embraced the European Union’s offer of “associate membership” after a two-day summit at which Brussels and Ottawa gave themselves until next June to work out what their new relationship will look like.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s endorsement of the proposal by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen followed weeks of hesitation, a hostile response from U.S. President Donald Trump and pushback from EU heavyweight Germany.

“In the coming months, we will determine the full substance, scale, and scope of this new form of membership,” Carney told a press conference on Friday at the end of the two-day summit at the Port of Montreal. 

“Today, we move towards associate membership for Canada,” Carney said, describing it as “the deepest possible partnership short of accession.”

The two sides have set a June 2027 deadline to determine the terms and boundaries of their intensifying relationship — an alliance that comes with a payment schedule. Carney danced around a question pressing him on how much associate membership will cost the Canadian public.

“We don’t view this as paying, personally,” Carney said, stressing the alliance as a “positive” project.

title: EU open to flexibility on euro and Schengen if UK tries to rejoin
content:
LONDON — Brussels would be flexible on letting Britain stay out of the euro and the Schengen area if it applied to rejoin the European Union, two EU officials familiar with the bloc’s approach have told POLITICO.

Britain would not necessarily have to join the single currency or passport-free zone — a concern held by some British voters — according to the two officials, who were granted anonymity to speak freely about a sensitive matter.

Opening the door for the U.K. to return to the bloc on similar terms would be a serious boost to the prospects of restoring the country’s EU membership, and a rejection of those who have argued it shouldn’t be allowed back in without joining the euro or Schengen.

U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Brexit isn’t working — and even suggested rejoining the EU could make it into Labour’s next election manifesto.

But some euroskeptics say a returning Britain would likely be strong-armed into making commitments to European integration that go beyond the membership deal it had before Brexit.

title: How Ireland plans to beat the data center backlash
content:
TALLAGHT, Ireland — In a suburban industrial park south of Dublin, a sprawling mass of tubes, vents and steel stretches as far as the eye can see, forming a dense web of gray monoliths that encircle the city.

As the EU’s tech capital, where most of the world’s technology giants have their European headquarters, Ireland was ground zero for the backlash against the energy-guzzling data centers needed to power the promised revolution of artificial intelligence.

Dublin is now leading an experiment within Europe to force tech firms to invest in renewable energy. As pushback spreads across Europe and data centers prove a hot-button issue for the U.S. midterm elections, that puts Ireland at the vanguard of countries globally that are trying to quell voter anger over financial and environmental disruptions caused by data centers.

Back in 2021, Ireland was far ahead of the curve in slamming the brakes on data centers as its utilities regulator almost entirely halted new facilities connecting to the creaking electricity grid around Dublin. Authorities warned that the exploding data center industry posed a “significant” risk to the security of the country’s electricity supply.

title: Carney frames C$1.6B AI investment as national security imperative
content:
MONTREAL — Prime Minister Mark Carney is positioning Ottawa’s C$1.6 billion investment in Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere as a downpayment on his country’s national security. 

“We’re not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know or … don’t trust,” Carney said Thursday in Montreal ahead of the start of the Canada-EU summit.

Carney framed the upcoming congress, which includes meetings Friday with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa, as a shared endeavor to build a stronger transatlantic alliance in the face of global disruption.

“Sovereignty now requires secure access to semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technology, vaccines, space-based communications and artificial intelligence,” Carney said. “Canada is taking a major step forward in artificial intelligence.”

In a pre-summit speech earlier Thursday in Montreal, von der Leyen cited April’s multi-billion dollar merger between Cohere and German counterpart Aleph Alpha as a key piece of the deepening Canada-EU cooperation that is set to unfold at Friday’s talks on AI.
